National Statistics Office (CSO) adopted the GVA in 2015 2. Income Method This method includes all the income generated by the factor of production which are inputs in the process of producing final goods or services, in the entire economy.
Components of Income Method
(a) Compensation to Employees: It refers to the total wages or salaries paid to workers for their product services.
(b) Operating Surplus: It refers to the profit earned by businesses (profit, rent and interest) after deducting employees compensation (wages).

(c) Mixed Income: It is the income earned by self-employed individuals and unincorporated businesses. It arises when elements of factor income (labour and capital) cannot be distinctly separated. E.g. A doctor running their own clinic.

blocks.text: Every economy faces three fundamental problems due to scarcity of resources:
What to Produce? Howto Produce? For Whom to Produce?
This problem refers to deciding which goods and services should be produced and in what quantity.
An economy must decide how its limited resources should be allocated between different types of goods.
Types of Final Goods
Finished goods that are used directly by individuals for personal consumption and are not used to produce other goods.
Example: Clothes, food, smartphones.
Goods that are used by businesses to produce other goods and services. They help in production and do not get consumed immediately.
Example: Machines used to produce T-shirts, factory equipment, tools.

Inventory elt refers to the items a business keeps in stock for sale or production purposes. It can include raw materials, work- in-progress items and finished goods, depending on the type of business. elf the sale of goods increases the inventory decumulates and if the sale of goods decreases the inventory accumulates. It can be either planned or unplanned.

Auxiliaries to trade refers to the factors that are essential for bringing the goods from the place of their production to the place of their consumption. In other words, these are essential services and functions that assist the business.
E.g. Transportation, communication, banking, insurance, warehousing, and advertising.

Does GDP Reflect the Welfare of Society?
Although GDP is an important indicator of economic growth and production, it does not fully reflect the welfare or well-being of society.

Limitations of GDP as a Measure of Welfare 1. Ignores Income Distribution GDP shows the total income of a country, but it does not indicate how that income is distributed among people. A country may have high GDP while many people \ poor.
2. Excludes Non-Market Activities
Activities such as household work, voluntary services, and caregiving contribute to welfare but are not included in GDP because they are not sold in the market.
3. Ignores Environmental Damage
Production that causes pollution or environmental degradation increases GDP but may reduce the overall quality of life.
4, Excludes Quality of Life Factors Sewell GDP does not consider health, education, leisure, safety, or happiness, which are important for social welfare.
5. Underground Economy Not Included
Economic activities in the informal or black market are generally not counted in GDP.
